title: Data breach compensation that companies rarely actually pay
p1:
A data breach happens. Millions of records are exposed. Then comes the question: "Will affected customers get compensation?"

The answer surprises many people: a breach does not automatically mean a payout.
p2:
Many assume companies must pay every person whose data was leaked. In reality, compensation usually depends on proving actual harm, such as financial loss, identity theft, or serious distress caused by the breach.

A leaked email address alone may not lead to a payment.
p3:
This is why many data breach claims fail or result in small settlements. The hardest part is not proving that data was exposed — it is connecting that exposure to a real impact.

For companies, the lesson is clear: protecting customer data is not only about avoiding fines. It is about maintaining trust before damage occurs.

For individuals, keeping records of suspicious activity after a breach can make a major difference if a claim becomes possible.
conclusion: Do you think companies should compensate customers automatically after a data breach, or only when people can prove actual harm?
